bib.title: HaluEval: A Large-Scale Hallucination Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), pages 6449-6464

question: What types of content, and to what extent, do LLMs hallucinate, and can LLMs recognize hallucinations in text?
hypothesis: Hallucinations are likely to appear in diverged and conflicting LLM responses (following Manakul et al., 2023), and LLMs are poor at recognising hallucinated text that closely resembles ground truth.
contributions: HaluEval: 35,000 hallucinated/normal samples: 5,000 general user queries with ChatGPT responses (human-annotated) and 30,000 task-specific examples (QA, knowledge-grounded dialogue, summarization).
A two-stage automatic sampling-then-filtering framework using ChatGPT to generate hallucinated samples.
Evaluation of 10 LLMs on hallucination recognition and three improvement strategies (knowledge retrieval, CoT, sample contrast).

method.summary: Task-specific hallucinated samples are generated by ChatGPT from seed data (HotpotQA, OpenDialKG, CNN/Daily Mail) with two sampling styles (one-pass and conversational instructions), then ChatGPT picks the more plausible of the two candidates (filtering). For general queries, 5,000 Alpaca queries with the lowest BERTScore similarity among three ChatGPT responses are human-annotated for hallucination. LLMs are then asked yes/no whether a sample contains hallucination.
method.task: hallucination recognition (binary classification) for QA, knowledge-grounded dialogue, summarization and general user queries

datasets.name: HotpotQA (seed for QA)
datasets.split: randomly sampled from the training set (part of 30,000 across three tasks)
datasets.preprocessing: hallucinated answer generated per question using 4 patterns (comprehension, factualness, specificity, inference)

datasets.name: OpenDialKG (seed for dialogue)
datasets.split: randomly sampled from the training set

datasets.name: CNN/Daily Mail (seed for summarization)
datasets.split: randomly sampled from the training set

datasets.name: Alpaca 52K instruction data (general user queries)
datasets.size: 5,000 queries retained from 52K, each with a ChatGPT response
datasets.preprocessing: 3 ChatGPT responses sampled per query; average pairwise BERTScore computed; 5,000 queries with lowest similarity retained; 3 human labelers per response, max-voting; 977 labeled hallucinated

other.use: generator and filter of hallucinated samples, also evaluated

inference.decoding: evaluation: temperature zero for all models; generation of hallucinated samples with Azure OpenAI ChatGPT API
inference.samples: For recognition, one randomly chosen output (hallucinated or normal) per sample is classified, single run; for general queries 3 ChatGPT responses are sampled per query for selection. No seeds or repeated runs stated.
inference.prompting: Few-shot instruction prompts with demonstrations per hallucination pattern; answer must be Yes or No (Tables 13-15). Sampling uses one-pass (full instruction at once) and conversational (instruction taught in parts) schemas; filtering is a judge prompt choosing between the two hallucinated candidates.
inference.retrieval: Knowledge-retrieval variant supplies ChatGPT with facts retrieved from Wikipedia (no retriever, k or index described); not used for summarization

parameters.hallucinated answer length: can only have about 5 more words than the right answer

metrics.name: Accuracy of hallucination classification
metrics.definition: percent of samples (hallucinated or right output, randomly one per sample) correctly labeled Yes/No for containing hallucination

metrics.name: Fleiss's kappa
metrics.definition: inter-annotator agreement of human labelers over 5,000 annotated samples

baselines: Random chance (50%) referenced in text; 10 LLMs compared
ChatGPT with Knowledge, CoT, Contrast variants
eval.protocol: Zero fine-tuning, temperature 0, single run, no significance tests. Human annotation: 30 labelers chosen by agreement with researcher labels on test examples, 3 labels per response, max-voting, labels cover unverifiable, non-factual, irrelevant.

prompts.text: I want you act as a hallucination answer generator. Given a question, right answer, and related knowledge, your objective is to write a hallucinated answer that sounds plausible but is factually incorrect. You SHOULD write the hallucinated answer using the following method (each with some examples): ... You should try your best to make the answer become hallucinated. #Hallucinated Answer# can only have about 5 more words than #Right Answer#. #Knowledge#: <insert the related knowledge> #Question#: <insert the question> #Right Answer#: <insert the right answer to the question> #Hallucinated Answer#:
prompts.where: Table 2, p.3 (pattern texts and demonstrations abbreviated; full in paper)

prompts.text: I want you act as an answer judge. Given a question, two answers, and related knowledge, your objective is to select the best and correct answer without hallucination and non-factual information. ... You MUST select an answer from the provided two answers. #Knowledge#: ... #Question#: ... #Answer 1#: <hallucinated answer, one-pass> #Answer 2#: <hallucinated answer, conversational> #Your Choice#:

I want you act as an answer judge. Given a question and an answer, your objective is to determine if the provided answer contains non-factual or hallucinated information. You SHOULD give your judgement based on the following hallucination types and the world knowledge. ... The answer you give MUST be "Yes" or "No". #Question#: <Here is the test question> #Answer#: <Here is the hallucinated answer or right answer> #Your Judgement#:

prompts.purpose: Sampling, filtering and recognition for dialogue and summarization
prompts.text: Analogous templates in Tables 9-12, 14, 15 (appendix); not reproduced here.

evidence.quote: We use a temperature of 1.0 to generate samples and set the maximum number of tokens for generation to 256.

results.claim: About 19.5% of annotated ChatGPT responses to general user queries contain hallucination.
results.setup: 5,000 Alpaca queries selected for lowest BERTScore similarity among three ChatGPT samples; three human labelers, max-voting; 977 labeled hallucinated
results.note: Selection of low-similarity queries biases toward hallucination-prone queries; rate does not generalise to all queries. Quote is the broken-line text 977 responses ... (19.5%).

results.claim: ChatGPT recognises hallucination in QA with only 62.59% accuracy.
results.setup: HaluEval QA, ChatGPT, temperature 0, few-shot judge prompt

results.claim: ChatGPT reaches only 58.53% accuracy on summarization hallucination recognition, barely above chance.
Claude 2 scores highest on QA recognition among evaluated models.
Alpaca (7B) is far below chance on QA recognition.
results.note: Likely reflects output-format or Yes/No bias failures rather than knowledge; the paper only says well below chance.

results.claim: GPT-3 (davinci) is around chance on QA.
On general user queries, ChatGPT scores 79.44% in Table 5 and 86.22% in Table 8.
results.note: Table 8 prints the same baseline ChatGPT General entry as 86.22; the paper does not explain the discrepancy.

results.claim: Retrieved Wikipedia knowledge raises ChatGPT QA recognition from 62.59 to 76.83.
results.setup: HaluEval QA, ChatGPT with retrieved knowledge

results.claim: Knowledge gives only a mild gain on dialogue (72.40 to 73.80).
results.table: Table 8, row w/ Knowledge, column Dialogue

results.claim: CoT lowers ChatGPT QA recognition to 59.58 but helps summarization (58.53 to 61.21).
results.note: Text says CoT mildly improves yet worsens QA and dialogue; summarization 61.21 from 58.53.

results.claim: Sample contrast (showing right and hallucinated samples together) is worst: 49.19 on QA.
results.table: Table 8, row w/ Contrast, column QA

results.claim: Fleiss's kappa between human labelers is 0.811.
results.setup: 5,000 annotated ChatGPT responses, three labelers each
results.note: Paper calls this perfect agreement; conventional scales call it almost perfect.

results.claim: ChatGPT fails to recognise 3109 QA, 891 dialogue and 3868 summarization samples; over half of failures are in pattern I.
results.setup: ChatGPT recognition failures by hallucination pattern (QA P-I 1559)

limits: Hallucinated samples are generated by ChatGPT, so quality is capped by its ability to follow the sampling instruction; the filter is also ChatGPT.
Benchmark measures recognition of hallucination, not generation rates or underlying causes (authors concede).
Generated hallucinated samples are close to ground truth and may be misused; authors say usage should be monitored.
No human validation of the 30,000 generated samples is reported; no repeated runs, seeds or significance tests.
Recognition is Yes/No with a randomly chosen hallucinated or right output per sample; very low scores of 7B open models (e.g. Alpaca 6.68 QA) are not diagnosed.
Table 5 and Table 8 print different ChatGPT General accuracies (79.44 vs 86.22).
Retrieval details (retriever, number of passages) are not given; 7B open models and 2023 API models (Claude, text-davinci) are dated.

terms.definition: content that conflicts with the source or cannot be verified by the factual knowledge
two-stage generation: diverse hallucination sampling with one-pass and conversational instructions, then selecting the most plausible and difficult hallucinated sample via a judge instruction

lineage.note: hallucinations appear in diverged responses, motivating low-similarity query selection
